correctness.rationale: Fix the exact word \(B=0\pi(T)\), justified by arXiv:2510.11318 Theorem 2. Every φ-image starts in 0 and any 1 or 2 is terminal, so T-adjacent pairs are contained in 00,01,02,10,20; all five occur in \(\varphi^4(0)\). Define \(W_a=\pi(\varphi^3(a))\), whose lengths are 20,17,11. Since \(T=\varphi^3(T)\), all B factors of lengths \(\le11\) are exhaustively covered by \(0W_0\) and \(W_aW_b\) for those five adjacent pairs. Exact enumeration of all these six short words gives \(P(1),\ldots,P(11)=(2,2,2,2,2,1,2,1,1,0,0)\), as recorded and reproduced by the checker. Missing length-10 and -11 centers prohibit all longer even and odd palindromes. Fifteen distinct palindromes have appeared by prefix length 25, but only fourteen by 24, proving the sharp defect \(N-15\) for \(N\ge25\). A separately implemented 100,000-symbol eertree agrees. Finite sampling is corroboration only; infinite exclusion comes from the finite-cover lemma.

value.rationale: Palindromic complexity and defect are standard intrinsic invariants of infinite words, and this exact Kimberling word was recently studied using morphic, factor-complexity, and critical-exponent tools. The classification shows that despite having ordinary factor complexity \(p(n)=2n\) for every n, its distinct palindrome collection is finite (15) and its palindromic defect grows linearly with an exact sharp starting threshold. This differs structurally from complement-symmetric Rote words with palindromes at every length. It is a complete natural classification, not an arbitrary finite prefix statistic or a consequence of a renaming of the known \(p(n)=2n\) result. Its significance is confined to this word; no downstream general theorem is asserted.
